92. 
93. `upool` *is* the module under verification, so these are **not** "trusted until upool
94. is verified" — they are design-forced thin-facade boundaries over the global frame allocator,
95. the same wording class as the `frame.rs` singleton wrappers (`frame::alloc` … "external_body
96. until the free-function layer is verified"). The verified part of `upool` is everything that
97. reasons through `UserFrame` (its `view`/`inv`, `new`, `address`, `leak`, `share`, `refcount`,
98. `drop` — all machine-verified) **plus the `Upool` type itself**; only the two `Upool` facade
99. methods, whose abstract state *is* the global `FrameAllocView` they do not own, stay trusted.
100. 
101. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::Upool` (struct) — **ELIMINATED** (no longer `external_body`).
102.   The type is now machine-verified (`#[verus_verify]`). It is never constructed in verified code
103.   (only the `external_body` `Upool::new` constructs it), so exposing its `()` field is harmless;
104.   its `View` remains `uninterp spec fn view() -> FrameAllocView`. Removing the attribute verifies
105.   cleanly (`make verify-kernel MODULE=mm::phys` → 86 verified, 0 errors).
106. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::Upool::new` — carries the **real** contract
107.   `ensures result@.wf()`. `FrameAllocView::wf()` is a non-trivial conjunction (page-alignment,
108.   allocated/free disjointness, allocated↔refcount consistency, u8-bounded refcounts) over the
109.   pool's *uninterpreted* `view()`; it is **unprovable from an uninterpreted view**, so the body
110.   is an assumed §8 ghost-attachment axiom (the pool introduces no frames of its own — `wf()` is
111.   the one fact its boot-time caller needs before handing the pool to `PhysMemoryManager::init`).
112.   Making the view spec-readable is impossible within the `upool` module: an interpreted view
113.   (`phys_view().frames`) makes `alloc`'s `alloc_one` transition self-contradictory (a 0-arg
114.   `uninterp phys_view()` is a logic constant, so `old(self)@ == final(self)@`), and a ghost field
115.   cannot be added because `FrameAllocView`/`Ghost<_>` do not exist in non-`verus` builds and a
116.   cfg-gated field would diverge the exec struct (ast-consistency violation). See
117.   `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-upool/verification_todo.md`.
118. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::Upool::alloc` — delegates to `frame::alloc` (itself
119.   `external_body`). Its postcondition speaks of `self@` (the uninterpreted pool view: the
120.   `alloc_one` free→allocated transition plus the empty-pool `Err` arm `free_count() == 0`),
121.   whereas `frame::alloc`'s contract speaks of `phys_view().frames`. Bridging `self@` to
122.   `phys_view().frames` is the **deferred §8 ghost token in the frame free-function layer**, so
123.   `alloc` stays `external_body` *until the frame free-function layer is verified* — exactly like
124.   its `frame.rs` siblings (`frame::alloc`/`book`/`share`), NOT "when upool is verified".
125. 
126. ## Cross-module dependencies trusted until their module is verified (`external_body` / `assume_specification`)
127. 
128. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init` — also listed under skip; callable from verified `init`.
129. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::init` — no specs yet; opaque callee.
130. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::map_frame` — exec-only helper holding the
131.   identity-mapping side effect extracted from `KernelFrame::new`. Declared in
132.   `kframe.spec.rs` as `pub assume_specification[ KernelFrame::map_frame ](base: FrameAddress)
133.   -> Result<(), Error>;` with an **empty** contract (no `requires`, no abstract `ensures`).
134.   Its sole effect is calling `mm::virt::identity_map_page`, whose precondition
135.   `identity_map_view().inv()` is a global invariant of the not-yet-verified `mm::virt` module.
136.   That invariant cannot be discharged from `mm::phys`: `identity_map_view` is an `uninterp spec
137.   fn` in the PRIVATE `mod identity_map` and is not re-exported, so it cannot even be NAMED here
138.   (verified: `grep identity_map_view` in `mm/virt/mod.rs` shows only `identity_map_page`,
139.   `memcpy`, `sync_kernel_pdes` are re-exported). This trusts strictly LESS than the previous
140.   `external_body` on `new`: the owned-frame identity (`kf@ == base@`) and well-formedness

125.             self.inv(),
126.         ensures
127.             result@ == self@,
128.             result.inv(),
129.     )]
130.     pub fn leak(self) -> FrameAddress {
131.         let this: ManuallyDrop<Self> = ManuallyDrop::new(self);
132.         this.addr
133.     }
134. 
135.     ///
136.     /// # Description
137.     ///
138.     /// Adds a new reference to the underlying physical frame and returns a fresh
139.     /// [`UserFrame`] handle that owns that reference. The two handles share the
140.     /// same physical frame, and the frame is only reclaimed once both handles are
141.     /// dropped.
142.     ///
143.     /// This is the building block for copy-on-write sharing: the parent retains
144.     /// its handle, the child receives the returned handle.
145.     ///
146.     /// # Returns
147.     ///
148.     /// On success, a new [`UserFrame`] that aliases the same physical frame as
149.     /// `self`. On failure, an error is returned.
150.     ///
151.     #[verus_spec(result =>
152.         requires
153.             self.inv(),
154.         ensures
155.             match result {
156.                 Ok(uf) => {
157.                     &&& uf@ == self@
158.                     &&& uf.inv()
159.                     &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
160.                 },
161.                 Err(_) => {
162.                     ||| !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
163.                     ||| crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@] >= 255
164.                 },
165.             },
166.     )]
167.     pub fn share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
168.         frame::share(self.addr)?;
169.         Ok(Self { addr: self.addr })
170.     }
171. 
172.     ///
173.     /// # Description
174.     ///
175.     /// Returns the current reference count of the underlying physical frame.
176.     ///
177.     /// # Returns
178.     ///
179.     /// Upon success, the current reference count of the underlying physical frame is returned.
180.     /// Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
181.     ///
182.     #[verus_spec(result =>
183.         requires
184.             self.inv(),
185.         ensures
186.             match result {
187.                 Ok(count) => {
188.                     &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
189.                     &&& count as int == crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@]
190.                 },
191.                 Err(_) => !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@),
192.             },
193.     )]
194.     pub fn refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error> {
195.         frame::refcount(self.addr)
196.     }
197. }
198.

200. impl Drop for UserFrame {
201.     #[verus_spec(
202.         opens_invariants none
203.         no_unwind
204.     )]
205.     fn drop(&mut self) {

207.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]

210.     }
211. }

215. //==================================================================================================
216.

218. /// # Description
219. ///
220. /// Thin facade over the module-level [`frame`](super::frame) allocator. Exists as a distinct type
221. /// so user-frame allocation has its own entry point ([`Upool::alloc`] returning [`UserFrame`]).
222. ///
223. #[derive(Debug)]
224. #[verus_verify]
225. pub struct Upool {
226.     /// Private field prevents external construction.
227.     _private: (),
228. }
229.

231. impl Upool {
232.     ///
233.     /// # Description
234.     ///
235.     /// Instantiates a user frame pool.
236.     ///
237.     /// # Returns
238.     ///
239.     /// A user frame pool.
240.     ///
241.     // Dependency contract: opaque pool facade whose real backing store is the global frame
242.     // allocator. `external_body` because `result@.wf()` is stated over the pool's *uninterpreted*
243.     // view (`FrameAllocView::wf()` cannot be derived from an uninterpreted `view()`), so the
244.     // body is an assumed §8 ghost-attachment axiom — the pool introduces no frames of its own;
245.     // `wf()` is the only fact its boot-time caller needs before handing the pool to
246.     // `PhysMemoryManager::init`. See `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md` and
247.     // `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-upool/verification_todo.md` for why the view cannot be made

249.     // transition soundness or requires a ghost field that does not exist in non-`verus` builds).
250.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
251.     #[verus_spec(result =>
252.         ensures
253.             result@.wf(),
254.     )]
255.     pub(super) fn new() -> Self {
256.         Self { _private: () }
257.     }
258. 
259.     ///

261.     ///
262.     /// Allocates a single user frame from the user frame pool.
263.     ///
264.     /// # Returns
265.     ///
266.     /// Upon success, a user frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
267.     ///

269.     // as a watermark-agnostic single-frame allocation over the pool's frame partition. Marked
270.     // `external_body` until the `frame` free-function layer is verified.
271.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
272.     #[verus_spec(result =>
273.         requires
274.             old(self)@.wf(),
275.         ensures
276.             final(self)@.wf(),
277.             match result {

285.                 },
286.             },
287.     )]

=== caller_analysis.md ===
# Caller Analysis: `mm::phys::upool`

## Script Output
See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-upool/find_callers_lsp.out`
(rust-analyzer LSP, intra-crate only; crate `kernel` has no external dependents).

Summary: 8 exec functions, all `pub`/`pub(super)`/trait-pub, 0 private, 2 types
(`UserFrame`, `Upool`). One implicit caller: `impl Drop for UserFrame`.

All callers live in the same crate, concentrated in:
- `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/vmem.rs` (mapping + copy-on-write fault resolution)
- `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/manager.rs` (fork / frame sharing)
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs` (bulk + single user-frame allocation)
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs` (boot-time pool construction)
- `src/kernel/src/mm/elf.rs` (segment loading — holds `Vec<UserFrame>`)

## Trait Obligations
- Trait: `Drop` for `UserFrame` — `drop(&mut self)` must release the handle's
  reference to the underlying physical frame (`frame::free`), reclaiming the frame
  only when the last reference is dropped. Callers depend on this for automatic
  cleanup on error paths, and deliberately **suppress** it (via `ManuallyDrop` or
  `leak`) whenever ownership is transferred elsewhere (page table) or the handle is
  only a transient *probe*. Errors inside `drop` are logged, not propagated (drop
  cannot fail).
- Trait: `View for UserFrame` — abstract value is `int`, the physical frame address
  (`self.addr@`). Callers reason about *which* frame a handle owns, never about the
  handle's internal layout.

## Caller Expectations

### `UserFrame::new(addr) -> Self`
- Callers assume: produces an owning handle whose `view == addr@`; no allocation,
  no refcount change, infallible.
- Used three distinct ways:
  - **Probe** wrapped in `ManuallyDrop` to call `refcount()`/`share()` without ever
    freeing (`vmem.rs:869`, `virt/manager.rs:349`).
  - **Take-ownership-to-free**: `drop(UserFrame::new(old_frame))` to decrement the
    refcount of a frame whose address was recovered from a PTE (`vmem.rs:895`).
  - **Re-wrap** an unmapped frame address back into an owning handle returned to the
    caller (`vmem.rs:1522`).
- Callers don't care about: how the address is stored; that it's just a thin wrapper.
- Would break callers: if `new` allocated, bumped a refcount, or returned a handle
  whose `view != addr@`.

### `UserFrame::address(&self) -> FrameAddress`
- Callers assume: pure read of the owned frame's physical address, no consume, no
  side effect, repeatable. Result feeds `page_table.map(...)` and `memcpy`
  (`vmem.rs:361,882,887`).
- Callers don't care about: internal representation; only that the returned address
  equals the handle's `view`.

### `UserFrame::leak(self) -> FrameAddress`
- Callers assume: consumes the handle and returns its address **without** running
  `Drop`/`frame::free`, transferring ownership of the frame to whoever now records
  the address (the page table). Used right after a successful `map` (`vmem.rs:368`,
  `vmem.rs:891`).
- Critical invariant: after `leak`, no decrement of the frame's refcount occurs from
  this handle. A regression that freed on leak would double-free once the page table
  is later torn down.
- Callers don't care about: the returned address in the `_ = leak()` case — they only
  need the suppress-drop effect.

### `UserFrame::share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
- Callers assume (success): the underlying frame's refcount is incremented and a
  **new** owning handle aliasing the same physical frame (`result@ == self@`) is
  returned. The two handles independently own one reference each; the frame survives
  until both are dropped.
- Callers assume (error): no new reference acquired, `self` and its frame unchanged —
  so the parent's existing mapping/refcount is untouched (`virt/manager.rs:350`, fork
  CoW path; the parent is held in `ManuallyDrop` so a `?` early-return cannot
  double-decrement).
- Callers don't care about: the mechanism of the refcount bump (`frame::share`).
- Would break callers: returning a handle to a *different* frame, or succeeding
  without actually incrementing the refcount (would cause premature free).

### `UserFrame::refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error>`
- Callers assume: returns the current reference count of the owned frame; does **not**
  consume or mutate the handle (`&self`), and (the probe is in `ManuallyDrop`) does not
  free. Used to detect the `== 1` last-reference fast path in CoW resolution
  (`vmem.rs:870`).
- Callers don't care about: anything but the numeric count for the owned frame.

### `Upool::new() -> Self`  *(pub(super))*
- Caller: boot-time `mm::phys` init (`mod.rs:185`), exactly once, before handing the
  pool to `PhysMemoryManager::init`.
- Callers assume: produces a valid pool facade with `@.wf()` holding so subsequent
  `alloc` preconditions are met. No parameters, infallible.
- Callers don't care about: the pool has no real state (`_private: ()`); the actual
  backing store is the global frame allocator.

### `Upool::alloc(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
- Caller: `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` (single) and the loop in
  `alloc_many_user_frames` (`manager.rs:238,290`), after the kernel-watermark check.
- Callers assume (success): one frame is removed from the pool's free partition and
  returned as an owning `UserFrame`; per the existing spec
  `old@.free_frames.contains(uf@)` and `final@ == old@.alloc_one(uf@)`,
  with `@.wf()` preserved.
- Callers assume (error): pool unchanged (`final@ == old@`) and the pool was empty
  (`old@.free_count() == 0`). The manager relies on this to restore state on bulk
  failure (`frames.clear()` + `lemma_user_bulk_err_restored`).
- Callers don't care about: that it delegates to `frame::alloc`.

## Abstract Resource
The module manages **user-space physical frames** drawn from the global frame
allocator, exposing them as **reference-counted owning handles** (`UserFrame`) plus a
thin per-pool allocation entry point (`Upool`). A `UserFrame` is the caller's RAII
proof of ownership of one reference to one physical frame; `Upool` is the watermark-
agnostic single-frame allocation facade over the pool's free partition.

## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
- A live `UserFrame` owns exactly one reference to the frame at its `view` address;
  the frame is not reclaimed while any handle still references it.
- `Drop` releases exactly one reference; `leak` transfers ownership without releasing;
  `ManuallyDrop` wrapping is the idiom for read-only probing (`refcount`/`share`)
  without affecting the count.
- `share` is the only operation that adds a reference, and it preserves the address
  (`result@ == self@`); `new`, `address`, `refcount`, and `leak` never change a
  frame's refcount.
- `Upool::alloc` conserves frames: success moves one frame from free to allocated
  (`alloc_one`), failure leaves the pool exactly as it was and signals exhaustion.
- A frame address round-trips faithfully through `new`/`address`/`leak`
  (`UserFrame::new(a).address()@ == a@`, `leak()@ == a@`), so callers can hand a frame
  to a page table and later re-wrap it for freeing without aliasing the wrong frame.

## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
- Source: added during top-down verification of `mm::phys` (manager/init paths).
- Functions WITH specs: `Upool::alloc` (full `requires`/`ensures` on `@.wf()`,
  `alloc_one`, empty-pool `Err` arm). `Upool`, `Upool::new`, and `Upool::alloc` are
  `external_body` and listed in `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md` (opaque pool facade /
  pool allocation primitive, "verified when `upool` is").
- Functions WITHOUT specs: `UserFrame::new`, `UserFrame::address`, `UserFrame::leak`,
  `UserFrame::share`, `UserFrame::refcount`, `UserFrame::drop`.
- View type: exists for both `UserFrame` (`= int`, the frame address, `closed`) and
  `Upool` (`= FrameAllocView`, `uninterp`). Do not modify these or the listed
  spec/view defs (`byte_at_address`, `FrameAllocView`, `FrameAllocView::wf`,
  `Inner::inv`, `frame_addr_of`, `View for Inner`, `Inner::internal_inv`).

### Assessment
- Coverage: **partial** — only `Upool::alloc` carries a contract; all `UserFrame`
  methods and `Upool::new` are unspecified despite real callers depending on their
  ownership/refcount semantics.
- Strength: `Upool::alloc`'s ensures is adequate (covers both arms incl. error-path
  state preservation and exhaustion). `Upool` being `external_body` means its abstract
  state is uninterpreted — acceptable per the TCB list, but `UserFrame` is *not*
  `external_body`, so its refcount-affecting methods (`share`, `drop`, `leak`) need
  specs to capture the per-frame reference-count discipline that CoW/fork callers rely
  on.
- View design: caller-abstract and stable — `UserFrame@` exposes only the frame
  address (exactly what every caller reasons about), not handle internals.

55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.

57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).

59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and

72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the

84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`

101. 
102. | Pattern | Policy |
103. |---|---|
104. | `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
105. | `assume(...)` | Banned |
106. | `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. 107. | `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
108. | `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
109. | `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
110. | `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |

127.   the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
128.   choose triggers automatically.

130.   to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

132. ## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)
133. 
134. Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
135. implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
136. FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
137. boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
138. list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
139. boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
140. TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

143. `axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.
144.

146. after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
147. record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:
148.

151. - Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
152. - Status: UNPROVEN
153. - Attempts: (list strategies tried)
154. - Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
155. ```

158. assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.
159.

161. gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`

163. proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.
164.

166.

168. whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
169. These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
170. unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.
171. 
172. **Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
173. Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
174. contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).
175.

177. search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
178. look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

181. 
182. vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
183. **Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
184. function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
185. the actual vstd source thoroughly:

187. ```bash

193. two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
194. `vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.
195.

197. - **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
198. - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
199.

201. 
202. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
203. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
204. claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
205. or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
206. strengthen the proof, do not change the code.
207.

212. `derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
213. Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
214. This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.
215.

217. 
218. ```rust
219. // ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
220. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
221.     #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
222.     { /* real implementation */ }
223.     #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
224.     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
225. }
226. ```
227. 
228. **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
229. 
230. ```rust

232. #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
233. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
234. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
235. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
236. ```
237. 
238. Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
239. meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

 Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
 two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
 `vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.
 
 - **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
 - **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
 - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
 
 ## Claiming Verus Limitations
 
 **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
 There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
 claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
 or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
 strengthen the proof, do not change the code.
 
 ### Guardrails
 
 **Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
 appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
 `derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
 Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
 This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.
 
 **Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
 
 ```rust
 // ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
     #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
     { /* real implementation */ }
     #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
 }
 ```
 
 **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
 
 ```rust

 #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
 #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
 ```
 
 Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
 meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

2. name: spec-drift-check
3. description: "Detect spec weakening via tree-sitter comparison against a baseline SHA. Use in specification, proving, and cheating-elimination phases to enforce that requires/ensures are never silently removed or relaxed."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Drift Check
7. 
8. ## What Is Spec Drift?
9. 
10. Spec drift occurs when a function's `requires` or `ensures` clauses are removed,
11. relaxed, or replaced with weaker versions during a pipeline phase. This is a
12. critical integrity violation because:
13. 
14. - **Callers depend on the spec.** Upstream modules may have already proven their
15.   correctness assuming the original spec. Weakening it silently breaks those proofs.
16. - **Weakening is never acceptable as a proof strategy.** If a spec is hard to
17.   prove, the proof needs strengthening, not the spec weakening.
18. 
19. ## When to Use
20. 
21. Use this skill in **every review** during these phases:
22. - **Specification** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
23. - **Proving** — compare specification END → current HEAD
24. - **Cheating Elimination** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
25. 
26. ## How to Run
27. 
28. ### Auto-detect mode (recommended)
29. 
30. The `check` subcommand reads `pipeline_state.json` to automatically determine
31. the module, source file, current phase, and baseline SHA:
32. 
33. ```bash
34. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check <module_name>
35. ```
36. 
37. ### Manual mode
38. 
39. Use `git-diff` when you need explicit control over the comparison range:
40. 
41. ```bash
42. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff <source_file> --before <baseline_sha> [--after <ref>]
43. ```
44. 
45. Where:
46. - `<source_file>` is the module's source file (relative to repo root)
47. - `<baseline_sha>` is the phase start SHA
48. - `--after` defaults to working tree if omitted
49. 
50. ### Exit Codes
51. - **0** — No contract drift detected ✅
52. - **1** — Contract drift detected ⚠ — spec weakening found
53. - **2** — Fatal error (tool failure)
54. 
55. ### Example
56. 
57. ```bash
58. # Auto-detect from pipeline state
59. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check libhfs-src-internal-volume_impl
60. 
61. # Manual comparison between two SHAs
62. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff src/libs/slab/src/lib.rs \
63.     --before abc1234 --after def5678
64. ```
65. 
66. ## What Counts as Contract Drift
67. 
68. | Change | Verdict | Reason |
69. |--------|---------|--------|
70. | `ensures` clause removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may depend on it |
71. | `ensures` clause replaced with weaker version | ⚠ FAIL | Reduces verification value |
72. | `requires` clause added | ⚠ FAIL | Shifts proof burden to callers |
73. | `requires` clause strengthened | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may not satisfy it |
74. | Spec/proof function body changed | ⚠ FAIL | May change meaning of specs |
75. | Dependency spec fn body changed | ⚠ FAIL | Effective contract of callers changed |
76. | Top-level entry spec changed vs base branch | ⚠ HARD FAIL | Never allowed — verification target |
77. | Function with specs removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers lose verified contract |
78. | `recommends` clause changed | ⚠ FAIL | May weaken soft preconditions |
79. | New `ensures` clause added | ✅ OK | Strengthens the contract |
80. | `requires` clause removed/relaxed | ✅ OK | Relaxes precondition for callers |
81. | Proof body changed (same spec) | ✅ OK | Only proof strategy changed |
82. 
83. ## Reviewer Checklist Item
84. 
85. When reviewing, verify:
86. 
87. 1. **Run the command.** Do not skip — check exit code.
88. 2. **If exit code 1:** Read the report. For each weakened function:
89.    - Is the original spec genuinely incorrect? If so, replace it with an
90.      equally strong (not weaker) correct spec.
91.    - Is this a proof difficulty workaround? **FAIL** — demand the
92.      original spec be restored and proven.
93. 3. **Document.** Record the drift check result in your review output.
94. 
95. ## Incorrect Spec vs Weakening
96. 
97. If a spec is genuinely wrong (e.g., encodes an incorrect formula or references
98. wrong fields), correct it. Note: if the code cannot satisfy a caller-required
99. spec, that is likely a **code bug**, not an incorrect spec. The correction must:
100. 1. Be equally strong — fix the error, do not weaken
101. 2. Still satisfy all caller expectations from `caller_analysis.md`
102. 
103. Weakening is **never** acceptable:
104. - "The proof is too hard" → strengthen the proof, not weaken the spec
105. - "Verus can't handle this" → use lemmas, external proof, or escalate
106. - "The caller doesn't actually need this" → the caller wrote their proof
107.   assuming the spec; removing it breaks their proof silently
108. 
109. ## Transitive Spec Drift
110. 
111. A function's effective contract includes the bodies of spec functions called
112. in its `requires`/`ensures`. The drift checker tracks these transitively
113. and flags `EFFECTIVE CONTRACT CHANGED` when a dependency spec fn
114. body is modified. Review these with the same rigor as direct clause changes.
115. 
116. ## Top-Level vs Internal Spec Drift
117. 
118. The pipeline distinguishes two levels of drift checking:
119. 
120. **Top-level entry point specs** are the functions listed in the verification
121. plan's `entries` field. These are always compared against the base branch.
122. Any change is a hard FAIL with no auto-fix.
123. 
124. **Internal module specs** are intermediate artifacts created to prove
125. top-level specs. The drift policy for internal specs:
126. 
127. - **Strengthening** (weaker precondition, stronger postcondition) is fine —
128.   this is normal refinement during proving.
129. - **Weakening** an existing spec may break callers further up the chain.
130.   If weakening is necessary, run a full `make verify` (not just the current
131.   module) to check that all callers still verify. If a caller breaks, adjust
132.   the caller to accommodate the change while still satisfying the top-level
133.   spec.
134.

1. ---
2. name: bug-reporting
3. description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Bug Reporting
7. 
8. Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
9. Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
10. to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.
11. 
12. ## Classification
13. 
14. After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
15. every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:
16. 
17. **True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
18. precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
19. logic error that always produces wrong results).
20. 
21. **Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
22. correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
23. a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
24. and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.
25. 
26. **False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
27. spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
28. limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).
29. 
30. ## When to Report
31. 
32. - **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
33. - **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
34.   needed and where they might come from.
35. - **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
36.   Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
37.   failure; see `verus-constraints`.
38. 
39. ## Auto-Fixable Bugs
40. 
41. Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
42. verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
43. the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
44. verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.
45. 
46. Auto-fixable categories:
47. - **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
48.   checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
49. - **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
50. - **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
51. - **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation
52. 
53. For each auto-fix:
54. 1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
55. 2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
56. 3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
57. 4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
58. 5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
59.    (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)
60. 
61. Do NOT auto-fix:
62. - Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
63. - Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
64. - Anything requiring architectural changes
65. - Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches
66. 
67. For these, report only — a human should decide.
68. 
69. ## Report Format
70. 
71. Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
72. Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
73. and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
74. 
75. ```markdown
76. ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
77. 
78. **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
79. **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
80. **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
81. verification command, and key error output.
82. **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
83. be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
84. **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
85. **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
86. **Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
87. ```
88. 
89. If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

 name: bug-reporting
 description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
 ---
 
 # Bug Reporting
 
 Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
 Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
 to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.
 
 ## Classification
 
 After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
 every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:
 
 **True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
 precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
 logic error that always produces wrong results).
 
 **Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
 correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
 a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
 and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.
 
 **False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
 spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
 limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).
 
 ## When to Report
 
 - **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
 - **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
   needed and where they might come from.
 - **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
   Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
   failure; see `verus-constraints`.
 
 ## Auto-Fixable Bugs
 
 Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
 verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
 the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
 verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.
 
 Auto-fixable categories:
 - **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
   checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
 - **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
 - **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
 - **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation
 
 For each auto-fix:
 1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
 2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
 3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
 4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
 5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
    (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)
 
 Do NOT auto-fix:
 - Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
 - Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
 - Anything requiring architectural changes
 - Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches
 
 For these, report only — a human should decide.
 
 ## Report Format
 
 Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
 Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
 and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
 
 ```markdown
 ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
 
 **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
 **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
 **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
 verification command, and key error output.
 **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
 be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
 **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
 **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
 **Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
 ```
 
 If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================

8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("upool.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("upool.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use crate::{
15.     hal::mem::FrameAddress,
16.     mm::phys::frame,
17. };
18. use ::core::mem::ManuallyDrop;
19. use ::sys::error::Error;
20. 
21. //==================================================================================================
22. // User Frame
23. //==================================================================================================
24. 
25. ///
26. /// # Description
27. ///
28. /// A type that represents a user frame.
29. ///
30. #[derive(Debug)]
31. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
32. pub struct UserFrame {
33.     /// Frame address.
34.     addr: FrameAddress,
35. }
36. 
37. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
38. verus! {
39. 
40. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
41. use crate::mm::phys::FrameAllocView;
42. 
43. /// Abstract view of a user frame: the physical address of the owned frame.
44. impl View for UserFrame {
45.     type V = int;
46. 
47.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
48.         self.addr@
49.     }
50. }
51. 
52. /// Abstract view of the user page pool: the frame partition it draws from.
53. ///
54. /// The `Upool` value carries no spec-readable state (its real backing store is the global
55. /// frame allocator), so its view is **uninterpreted**. The trust obligation therefore lives
56. /// on the two facade methods (`new`, `alloc`), whose abstract contracts speak of this
57. /// uninterpreted view and are pinned to the global allocator by the §8 ghost token in the
58. /// frame free-function layer. The `Upool` *type* itself is verified (not `external_body`):
59. /// it is never constructed in verified code, so its `()` field is harmless to expose.
60. impl View for Upool {
61.     type V = FrameAllocView;
62. 
63.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> FrameAllocView;
64. }
65. 
66. } // verus!
67. 
68. #[verus_verify]
69. impl UserFrame {
70.     ///
71.     /// # Description
72.     ///
73.     /// Instantiates a user frame.
74.     ///
75.     /// # Parameters
76.     ///
77.     /// - `addr`: Frame address.
78.     ///
79.     /// # Returns
80.     ///
81.     /// A user frame.
82.     ///
83.     #[verus_spec(result =>
84.         requires
85.             addr.inv(),
86.         ensures
87.             result@ == addr@,
88.             result.inv(),
89.     )]
90.     pub fn new(addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
91.         Self { addr }
92.     }
93. 
94.     ///
95.     /// # Description
96.     ///
97.     /// Returns the physical address of the target user frame.
98.     ///
99.     /// # Returns
100.     ///
101.     /// The physical address of the target user frame.
102.     ///
103.     #[verus_spec(result =>
104.         requires
105.             self.inv(),
106.         ensures
107.             result@ == self@,
108.             result.inv(),
109.     )]
110.     pub fn address(&self) -> FrameAddress {
111.         self.addr
112.     }
113. 
114.     ///
115.     /// # Description
116.     ///
117.     /// Consumes the user frame without freeing the underlying physical frame.
118.     ///
119.     /// # Returns
120.     ///
121.     /// The frame address.
122.     ///
123.     #[verus_spec(result =>
124.         requires
125.             self.inv(),
126.         ensures
127.             result@ == self@,
128.             result.inv(),
129.     )]
130.     pub fn leak(self) -> FrameAddress {
131.         let this: ManuallyDrop<Self> = ManuallyDrop::new(self);
132.         this.addr
133.     }
134. 
135.     ///
136.     /// # Description
137.     ///
138.     /// Adds a new reference to the underlying physical frame and returns a fresh
139.     /// [`UserFrame`] handle that owns that reference. The two handles share the
140.     /// same physical frame, and the frame is only reclaimed once both handles are
141.     /// dropped.
142.     ///
143.     /// This is the building block for copy-on-write sharing: the parent retains
144.     /// its handle, the child receives the returned handle.
145.     ///
146.     /// # Returns
147.     ///
148.     /// On success, a new [`UserFrame`] that aliases the same physical frame as
149.     /// `self`. On failure, an error is returned.
150.     ///
151.     #[verus_spec(result =>
152.         requires
153.             self.inv(),
154.         ensures
155.             match result {
156.                 Ok(uf) => {
157.                     &&& uf@ == self@
158.                     &&& uf.inv()
159.                     &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
160.                 },
161.                 Err(_) => {
162.                     ||| !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
163.                     ||| crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@] >= 255
164.                 },
165.             },
166.     )]
167.     pub fn share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
168.         frame::share(self.addr)?;
169.         Ok(Self { addr: self.addr })
170.     }
171. 
172.     ///
173.     /// # Description
174.     ///
175.     /// Returns the current reference count of the underlying physical frame.
176.     ///
177.     /// # Returns
178.     ///
179.     /// Upon success, the current reference count of the underlying physical frame is returned.
180.     /// Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
181.     ///
182.     #[verus_spec(result =>
183.         requires
184.             self.inv(),
185.         ensures
186.             match result {
187.                 Ok(count) => {
188.                     &&& crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
189.                     &&& count as int == crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@]
190.                 },
191.                 Err(_) => !crate::mm::phys::phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@),
192.             },
193.     )]
194.     pub fn refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error> {
195.         frame::refcount(self.addr)
196.     }
197. }
198. 
199. #[verus_verify]
200. impl Drop for UserFrame {
201.     #[verus_spec(
202.         opens_invariants none
203.         no_unwind
204.     )]
205.     fn drop(&mut self) {
206.         if let Err(e) = frame::free(self.addr) {
207.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
208.             error!("failed to free user frame: {:?}", e);
209.         }
210.     }
211. }
212. 
213. //==================================================================================================
214. // User Frame Pool
215. //==================================================================================================
216. 
217. ///
218. /// # Description
219. ///
220. /// Thin facade over the module-level [`frame`](super::frame) allocator. Exists as a distinct type
221. /// so user-frame allocation has its own entry point ([`Upool::alloc`] returning [`UserFrame`]).
222. ///
223. #[derive(Debug)]
224. #[verus_verify]
225. pub struct Upool {
226.     /// Private field prevents external construction.
227.     _private: (),
228. }
229. 
230. #[verus_verify]
231. impl Upool {
232.     ///
233.     /// # Description
234.     ///
235.     /// Instantiates a user frame pool.
236.     ///
237.     /// # Returns
238.     ///
239.     /// A user frame pool.
240.     ///
241.     // Dependency contract: opaque pool facade whose real backing store is the global frame
242.     // allocator. `external_body` because `result@.wf()` is stated over the pool's *uninterpreted*
243.     // view (`FrameAllocView::wf()` cannot be derived from an uninterpreted `view()`), so the
244.     // body is an assumed §8 ghost-attachment axiom — the pool introduces no frames of its own;
245.     // `wf()` is the only fact its boot-time caller needs before handing the pool to
246.     // `PhysMemoryManager::init`. See `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md` and
247.     // `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-upool/verification_todo.md` for why the view cannot be made
248.     // spec-readable within the `upool` module (an interpreted view either breaks `alloc`'s
249.     // transition soundness or requires a ghost field that does not exist in non-`verus` builds).
250.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
251.     #[verus_spec(result =>
252.         ensures
253.             result@.wf(),
254.     )]
255.     pub(super) fn new() -> Self {
256.         Self { _private: () }
257.     }
258. 
259.     ///
260.     /// # Description
261.     ///
262.     /// Allocates a single user frame from the user frame pool.
263.     ///
264.     /// # Returns
265.     ///
266.     /// Upon success, a user frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
267.     ///
268.     // Dependency contract: delegates to the global frame allocator (`frame::alloc`). Modeled
269.     // as a watermark-agnostic single-frame allocation over the pool's frame partition. Marked
270.     // `external_body` until the `frame` free-function layer is verified.
271.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
272.     #[verus_spec(result =>
273.         requires
274.             old(self)@.wf(),
275.         ensures
276.             final(self)@.wf(),
277.             match result {
278.                 Ok(uf) => {
279.                     &&& old(self)@.free_frames.contains(uf@)
280.                     &&& final(self)@ == old(self)@.alloc_one(uf@)
281.                 },
282.                 Err(_) => {
283.                     &&& final(self)@ == old(self)@
284.                     &&& old(self)@.free_count() == 0
285.                 },
286.             },
287.     )]
288.     pub fn alloc(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
289.         let addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc()?;
290.         Ok(UserFrame::new(addr))
291.     }
292. }

2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88. 
89. ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
90. 
91. 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
92.    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
93.    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
94.    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
95.    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
96.    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
97.    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
98.    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
99.    
100.    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
101.    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
102. 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
103.    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
104.    spec or proof instead.
105.    
106.    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
107.    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
108.      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
109.      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
110. 
111.    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
112. 
113.    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
114.       in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
115.       `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
116.       reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
117.       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
118.       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
119.    2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
120.       guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
121.       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
122.       Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
123.       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
124.       callers will not check it.
125.    3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
126.       compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
127.       explicitly in the spec.
128.    4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
129.       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
130.       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"

 ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
 
 ### Qualities of a Good Spec
 
 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,

    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.

    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
    recursive spec functions.
 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
 
 ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
 
 If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
 nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
 spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
 design model.
 
 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
    annotation beats no annotation.
 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
    Always search vstd first.
 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
    by vstd.
    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
    make Verus pass.
    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
 
 ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
 
 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
    
    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
    spec or proof instead.

    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments

       reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
    2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly

       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
       Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
       callers will not check it.

1. # Caller Analysis: `mm::phys::upool`
2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-upool/find_callers_lsp.out`
5. (rust-analyzer LSP, intra-crate only; crate `kernel` has no external dependents).
6. 
7. Summary: 8 exec functions, all `pub`/`pub(super)`/trait-pub, 0 private, 2 types
8. (`UserFrame`, `Upool`). One implicit caller: `impl Drop for UserFrame`.
9. 
10. All callers live in the same crate, concentrated in:
11. - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/vmem.rs` (mapping + copy-on-write fault resolution)
12. - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/manager.rs` (fork / frame sharing)
13. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs` (bulk + single user-frame allocation)
14. - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs` (boot-time pool construction)
15. - `src/kernel/src/mm/elf.rs` (segment loading — holds `Vec<UserFrame>`)
16. 
17. ## Trait Obligations
18. - Trait: `Drop` for `UserFrame` — `drop(&mut self)` must release the handle's
19.   reference to the underlying physical frame (`frame::free`), reclaiming the frame
20.   only when the last reference is dropped. Callers depend on this for automatic
21.   cleanup on error paths, and deliberately **suppress** it (via `ManuallyDrop` or
22.   `leak`) whenever ownership is transferred elsewhere (page table) or the handle is
23.   only a transient *probe*. Errors inside `drop` are logged, not propagated (drop
24.   cannot fail).
25. - Trait: `View for UserFrame` — abstract value is `int`, the physical frame address
26.   (`self.addr@`). Callers reason about *which* frame a handle owns, never about the
27.   handle's internal layout.
28. 
29. ## Caller Expectations
30. 
31. ### `UserFrame::new(addr) -> Self`
32. - Callers assume: produces an owning handle whose `view == addr@`; no allocation,
33.   no refcount change, infallible.
34. - Used three distinct ways:
35.   - **Probe** wrapped in `ManuallyDrop` to call `refcount()`/`share()` without ever
36.     freeing (`vmem.rs:869`, `virt/manager.rs:349`).
37.   - **Take-ownership-to-free**: `drop(UserFrame::new(old_frame))` to decrement the
38.     refcount of a frame whose address was recovered from a PTE (`vmem.rs:895`).
39.   - **Re-wrap** an unmapped frame address back into an owning handle returned to the
40.     caller (`vmem.rs:1522`).
41. - Callers don't care about: how the address is stored; that it's just a thin wrapper.
42. - Would break callers: if `new` allocated, bumped a refcount, or returned a handle
43.   whose `view != addr@`.
44. 
45. ### `UserFrame::address(&self) -> FrameAddress`
46. - Callers assume: pure read of the owned frame's physical address, no consume, no
47.   side effect, repeatable. Result feeds `page_table.map(...)` and `memcpy`
48.   (`vmem.rs:361,882,887`).
49. - Callers don't care about: internal representation; only that the returned address
50.   equals the handle's `view`.
51. 
52. ### `UserFrame::leak(self) -> FrameAddress`
53. - Callers assume: consumes the handle and returns its address **without** running
54.   `Drop`/`frame::free`, transferring ownership of the frame to whoever now records
55.   the address (the page table). Used right after a successful `map` (`vmem.rs:368`,
56.   `vmem.rs:891`).
57. - Critical invariant: after `leak`, no decrement of the frame's refcount occurs from
58.   this handle. A regression that freed on leak would double-free once the page table
59.   is later torn down.
60. - Callers don't care about: the returned address in the `_ = leak()` case — they only
61.   need the suppress-drop effect.
62. 
63. ### `UserFrame::share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
64. - Callers assume (success): the underlying frame's refcount is incremented and a
65.   **new** owning handle aliasing the same physical frame (`result@ == self@`) is
66.   returned. The two handles independently own one reference each; the frame survives
67.   until both are dropped.
68. - Callers assume (error): no new reference acquired, `self` and its frame unchanged —
69.   so the parent's existing mapping/refcount is untouched (`virt/manager.rs:350`, fork
70.   CoW path; the parent is held in `ManuallyDrop` so a `?` early-return cannot
71.   double-decrement).
72. - Callers don't care about: the mechanism of the refcount bump (`frame::share`).
73. - Would break callers: returning a handle to a *different* frame, or succeeding
74.   without actually incrementing the refcount (would cause premature free).
75. 
76. ### `UserFrame::refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error>`
77. - Callers assume: returns the current reference count of the owned frame; does **not**
78.   consume or mutate the handle (`&self`), and (the probe is in `ManuallyDrop`) does not
79.   free. Used to detect the `== 1` last-reference fast path in CoW resolution
80.   (`vmem.rs:870`).
81. - Callers don't care about: anything but the numeric count for the owned frame.
82. 
83. ### `Upool::new() -> Self`  *(pub(super))*
84. - Caller: boot-time `mm::phys` init (`mod.rs:185`), exactly once, before handing the
85.   pool to `PhysMemoryManager::init`.
86. - Callers assume: produces a valid pool facade with `@.wf()` holding so subsequent
87.   `alloc` preconditions are met. No parameters, infallible.
88. - Callers don't care about: the pool has no real state (`_private: ()`); the actual
89.   backing store is the global frame allocator.
90. 
91. ### `Upool::alloc(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
92. - Caller: `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` (single) and the loop in
93.   `alloc_many_user_frames` (`manager.rs:238,290`), after the kernel-watermark check.
94. - Callers assume (success): one frame is removed from the pool's free partition and
95.   returned as an owning `UserFrame`; per the existing spec
96.   `old@.free_frames.contains(uf@)` and `final@ == old@.alloc_one(uf@)`,
97.   with `@.wf()` preserved.
98. - Callers assume (error): pool unchanged (`final@ == old@`) and the pool was empty
99.   (`old@.free_count() == 0`). The manager relies on this to restore state on bulk
100.   failure (`frames.clear()` + `lemma_user_bulk_err_restored`).
101. - Callers don't care about: that it delegates to `frame::alloc`.
102. 
103. ## Abstract Resource
104. The module manages **user-space physical frames** drawn from the global frame
105. allocator, exposing them as **reference-counted owning handles** (`UserFrame`) plus a
106. thin per-pool allocation entry point (`Upool`). A `UserFrame` is the caller's RAII
107. proof of ownership of one reference to one physical frame; `Upool` is the watermark-
108. agnostic single-frame allocation facade over the pool's free partition.
109. 
110. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
111. - A live `UserFrame` owns exactly one reference to the frame at its `view` address;
112.   the frame is not reclaimed while any handle still references it.
113. - `Drop` releases exactly one reference; `leak` transfers ownership without releasing;
114.   `ManuallyDrop` wrapping is the idiom for read-only probing (`refcount`/`share`)
115.   without affecting the count.
116. - `share` is the only operation that adds a reference, and it preserves the address
117.   (`result@ == self@`); `new`, `address`, `refcount`, and `leak` never change a
118.   frame's refcount.
119. - `Upool::alloc` conserves frames: success moves one frame from free to allocated
120.   (`alloc_one`), failure leaves the pool exactly as it was and signals exhaustion.
121. - A frame address round-trips faithfully through `new`/`address`/`leak`
122.   (`UserFrame::new(a).address()@ == a@`, `leak()@ == a@`), so callers can hand a frame
123.   to a page table and later re-wrap it for freeing without aliasing the wrong frame.
124. 
125. ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
126. - Source: added during top-down verification of `mm::phys` (manager/init paths).
127. - Functions WITH specs: `Upool::alloc` (full `requires`/`ensures` on `@.wf()`,
128.   `alloc_one`, empty-pool `Err` arm). `Upool`, `Upool::new`, and `Upool::alloc` are
129.   `external_body` and listed in `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md` (opaque pool facade /
130.   pool allocation primitive, "verified when `upool` is").
131. - Functions WITHOUT specs: `UserFrame::new`, `UserFrame::address`, `UserFrame::leak`,

 - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/vmem.rs` (mapping + copy-on-write fault resolution)
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/manager.rs` (fork / frame sharing)
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs` (bulk + single user-frame allocation)
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs` (boot-time pool construction)

 ## Trait Obligations
 - Trait: `Drop` for `UserFrame` — `drop(&mut self)` must release the handle's
   reference to the underlying physical frame (`frame::free`), reclaiming the frame
   only when the last reference is dropped. Callers depend on this for automatic
   cleanup on error paths, and deliberately **suppress** it (via `ManuallyDrop` or
   `leak`) whenever ownership is transferred elsewhere (page table) or the handle is
   only a transient *probe*. Errors inside `drop` are logged, not propagated (drop
   cannot fail).
 - Trait: `View for UserFrame` — abstract value is `int`, the physical frame address
   (`self.addr@`). Callers reason about *which* frame a handle owns, never about the
   handle's internal layout.

 ### `UserFrame::new(addr) -> Self`
 - Callers assume: produces an owning handle whose `view == addr@`; no allocation,
   no refcount change, infallible.
 - Used three distinct ways:
   - **Probe** wrapped in `ManuallyDrop` to call `refcount()`/`share()` without ever
     freeing (`vmem.rs:869`, `virt/manager.rs:349`).
   - **Take-ownership-to-free**: `drop(UserFrame::new(old_frame))` to decrement the
     refcount of a frame whose address was recovered from a PTE (`vmem.rs:895`).
   - **Re-wrap** an unmapped frame address back into an owning handle returned to the
     caller (`vmem.rs:1522`).
 - Callers don't care about: how the address is stored; that it's just a thin wrapper.
 - Would break callers: if `new` allocated, bumped a refcount, or returned a handle
   whose `view != addr@`.
 
 ### `UserFrame::address(&self) -> FrameAddress`
 - Callers assume: pure read of the owned frame's physical address, no consume, no
   side effect, repeatable. Result feeds `page_table.map(...)` and `memcpy`
   (`vmem.rs:361,882,887`).
 - Callers don't care about: internal representation; only that the returned address
   equals the handle's `view`.
 
 ### `UserFrame::leak(self) -> FrameAddress`
 - Callers assume: consumes the handle and returns its address **without** running
   `Drop`/`frame::free`, transferring ownership of the frame to whoever now records
   the address (the page table). Used right after a successful `map` (`vmem.rs:368`,
   `vmem.rs:891`).

   this handle. A regression that freed on leak would double-free once the page table
   is later torn down.

   need the suppress-drop effect.

 - Callers assume (success): the underlying frame's refcount is incremented and a
   **new** owning handle aliasing the same physical frame (`result@ == self@`) is
   returned. The two handles independently own one reference each; the frame survives
   until both are dropped.

   so the parent's existing mapping/refcount is untouched (`virt/manager.rs:350`, fork
   CoW path; the parent is held in `ManuallyDrop` so a `?` early-return cannot
   double-decrement).

   without actually incrementing the refcount (would cause premature free).

 - Callers assume: returns the current reference count of the owned frame; does **not**
   consume or mutate the handle (`&self`), and (the probe is in `ManuallyDrop`) does not
   free. Used to detect the `== 1` last-reference fast path in CoW resolution

   pool to `PhysMemoryManager::init`.
 - Callers assume: produces a valid pool facade with `@.wf()` holding so subsequent
   `alloc` preconditions are met. No parameters, infallible.
 - Callers don't care about: the pool has no real state (`_private: ()`); the actual
   backing store is the global frame allocator.

 - Caller: `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` (single) and the loop in
   `alloc_many_user_frames` (`manager.rs:238,290`), after the kernel-watermark check.
 - Callers assume (success): one frame is removed from the pool's free partition and
   returned as an owning `UserFrame`; per the existing spec
   `old@.free_frames.contains(uf@)` and `final@ == old@.alloc_one(uf@)`,
   with `@.wf()` preserved.

   (`old@.free_count() == 0`). The manager relies on this to restore state on bulk
   failure (`frames.clear()` + `lemma_user_bulk_err_restored`).
 - Callers don't care about: that it delegates to `frame::alloc`.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 The module manages **user-space physical frames** drawn from the global frame
 allocator, exposing them as **reference-counted owning handles** (`UserFrame`) plus a
 thin per-pool allocation entry point (`Upool`). A `UserFrame` is the caller's RAII
 proof of ownership of one reference to one physical frame; `Upool` is the watermark-
 agnostic single-frame allocation facade over the pool's free partition.
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 - A live `UserFrame` owns exactly one reference to the frame at its `view` address;
   the frame is not reclaimed while any handle still references it.
 - `Drop` releases exactly one reference; `leak` transfers ownership without releasing;
   `ManuallyDrop` wrapping is the idiom for read-only probing (`refcount`/`share`)
   without affecting the count.
 - `share` is the only operation that adds a reference, and it preserves the address
   (`result@ == self@`); `new`, `address`, `refcount`, and `leak` never change a
   frame's refcount.

   (`alloc_one`), failure leaves the pool exactly as it was and signals exhaustion.

   (`UserFrame::new(a).address()@ == a@`, `leak()@ == a@`), so callers can hand a frame
   to a page table and later re-wrap it for freeing without aliasing the wrong frame.

   `UserFrame::share`, `UserFrame::refcount`, `UserFrame::drop`.

   `Upool` (`= FrameAllocView`, `uninterp`). Do not modify these or the listed
   spec/view defs (`byte_at_address`, `FrameAllocView`, `FrameAllocView::wf`,
   `Inner::inv`, `frame_addr_of`, `View for Inner`, `Inner::internal_inv`).

   methods and `Upool::new` are unspecified despite real callers depending on their
   ownership/refcount semantics.
